result:
That read is half right, but there's a mix-up in it worth clearing up before anything else: you don't need to train anything to make your makerspace assistant call tools well.

The RL training (PPO and all) already happened at the company that built the model you'll be calling — that's part of *how* it got good at using tools in the first place. You're not building a model from scratch; you're calling one that's already trained, the same way you'd call a web API in your class project. So "derive PPO and train my own model" isn't actually the step that gets your assistant calling tools better.

Here's the tempting part: you read "best agents use RL" and reasonably jumped to "so I should do RL too." But what actually moves the needle for your project is stuff fully within your control without any training: how clearly you describe each tool (what it does, what arguments it takes, when to use it), and how you phrase the request so the model reaches for the right one. Example: a tool documented as `check_calendar(date)` with no description of what it returns will get misused way more than one documented as `check_calendar(date) → list of open equipment slots for that date; call this before booking`. Same model, same training, very different success rate — because the fix is in your tool design, not in retraining anything.

This is also exactly the line your mission draws: training and the math inside models is explicitly out of scope — you're building the agent's architecture, not the model underneath it.

Does that distinction click — model training vs. writing a good tool description for a model that's already trained?
